newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Concern for Rwanda refugees in Tanzania, Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Concern for Rwanda refugees in Tanzania, Rwanda.

text.p: Suspected Tanzanian police burned down a church and beat Rwandan refugees sheltering inside to make them join the mass return of Hutus to Rwanda, aid officials said on Friday.
In Geneva, the U.N. refugee agency said it was concerned at reports at least 150 Rwandan returnees from Tanzania had been arrested based on neighbours' suspicions of their role in the 1994 genocide.

The aid officials in Tanzania said 28 Rwandan Hutu refugees staying at the church in the deserted Benaco refugee camp were attacked at night and forced to join a column of refugees trekking towards the Rusumo border crossing into Rwanda.
"Someone went in there and beat them. The church was burned down. No bodies were found," said a U.N. official in Ngara.
The aid officials, who declined to be identified, said suspicion for the attack rested on a Tanzanian police unit. The refugees had said they were waiting for God's word to return.
More than 260,000 refugees have gone back to Rwanda from Tanzania since last Saturday. Tanzanian authorities ordered all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return home by the end of December.

Tanzanian security officials were not available for comment. Staff of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) went to investigate the beating report and said the incident may have happened on Wednesday night.
In Geneva, UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole, citing reports from Murambi and Nyagatare in northeast Rwanda, said returnees were arrested in the last few days, accused by other villagers.

"We've heard reports that on returning to their communes in some areas, people are being arrested as suspected genocide perpetrators on the basis of accusations levelled by individual members of the public," O'Toole said.
"We are raising this issue with the Rwandan government and pointing out that Rwandan law stipulates that any arrest should only be carried out in accordance with proper legal procedures.
"Under Rwandan law, a warrant should be issued on the basis of a prepared file before someone is arrested," she added.

U.N. officials said on Friday the first genocide trials in Rwanda would start on December 30 in Kigali with two suspects accused of genocide and crimes against humanity, which carry a maximum sentence of death.

In another development, aid officials said they had found the bodies of three refugees apparently killed by machete blows in northwest Tanzania. The body of a 15-year-old was found near Lumasi camp and two other corpses were dumped near Benaco.
It was unclear who was responsible but in eastern Zaire last month Rwandan Hutu intimidators refusing to go to Rwanda killed refugees to force others to follow them.

Hutu hardliners, including former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen, refuse to return because they could face jail or death in Rwanda for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates in 1994.
Hundreds of thousands of refugees, urged on by intimidators, fled the camps and headed deeper into Tanzania last week. But police and troops, at times wielding sticks, turned most around.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said more than 12,000 refugees crossed into Rwanda from Tanzania on Friday, making a total of 266,000 to have returned since December 14.
UNHCR officials expected a 50-km (30-mile) column of more than 100,000 refugees to start arriving at the Rusumo crossing on Saturday. Many are exhausted after walking for six days.
